title: Lesson 13 - Multi-Source FlexCard Design: Layering Data and Elements
description: Guide in designing Flexcards to display relevant information from multiple data sources using existing or available elements (inputs, menu, data tables, charts, etc.) ensuring the data is presented clearly and logically based on the user's role and context.

questions.question: A FlexCard must show an account's key fields, a table of its contacts, and a chart of opportunities by stage. How should the data be assembled?
options: Three independent Turbo Extracts bound to three elements
An Integration Procedure that merges the account, contacts, and aggregated opportunity data into one payload
Static JSON for all three sections
A single standard Extract returning one flat list
questions.explanation: The card needs multiple data shapes, including a nested collection and an aggregated series, so an Integration Procedure should assemble them into one payload the card binds to. Independent Turbo Extracts would not produce the nested and aggregated shapes cleanly. Static JSON cannot reflect live data, and a single flat Extract cannot produce the required structure.

questions.question: Which element is the correct choice for showing a collection of related records on a FlexCard?
questions.explanation: A collection of related records is tabular data, so a data table is the correct element. A text element shows a single value, an input captures one value, and a menu selects from discrete options; none of them present a collection clearly.

questions.question: A consultant is designing a card and wants the user to understand what record it is about before seeing detail. What is the correct layout principle?
options: Lead with the chart so the data is prominent
Lead with identity, then key facts, then supporting detail, then actions
Put all data in one data table
Place the actions at the top
questions.explanation: A logical top-to-bottom order leads with identity so the user knows what the card is about, then key facts, then supporting detail, then actions. Leading with a chart before context forces the user to hunt for what the record is. One data table cannot hold mixed data types, and actions belong after the content they act on.
